meta.title: Culinary Oil Smoke Point, Thermal Stability & Toxic Aldehyde Formation Kinetic Database
leadStandards: Codex Alimentarius Standard for Named Vegetable Oils (CXS 210-1999)
International Olive Council (IOC) Commercial Quality Standards
European Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/343 (Discarded Frying Oil TPM Limits: 24-27%)
IARC Monograph Vol. 95 (Household Cooking with Frying Oils and Carcinogenic Aldehydes)

hne.name: 4-Hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE)
hne.origin: Peroxidative thermal cleavage of omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (linoleic acid).
hne.toxicity: Potent electrophilic cytotoxic alkenal. Readily forms covalent Michael adducts with cysteine, lysine, and histidine residues of cellular enzymes. Inhibits mitochondrial respiration, induces vascular endothelial oxidative stress, and is directly implicated in atherosclerosis and hepatic inflammation.

mda.name: Malondialdehyde (MDA)
mda.origin: Decomposition of prostaglandin-like bicyclic endoperoxides during lipid peroxidation.
mda.toxicity: Mutagenic dialdehyde. Reacts with deoxyguanosine in genomic DNA to synthesize mutagenic M1G adducts (pyrimido[1,2-a]purin-10(3H)-one), inducing replication arrest, frameshift mutations, and genomic instability.

acrolein.name: Acrolein (2-propenal)
acrolein.origin: Thermal cleavage of glycerol at temperatures approaching or exceeding oil smoke points, accelerated by polyunsaturated breakdown.
acrolein.toxicity: Highly reactive, volatile alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehyde and potent lacrimator. IARC Group 2A probable human carcinogen. Causes immediate upper respiratory epithelial necrosis, cilia paralysis, and has been epidemiologically linked to high rates of lung adenocarcinoma among domestic and commercial wok/fry cooks.

tpm.name: Total Polar Materials (TPM / TPC)
tpm.definition: The cumulative percentage of triglycerides that have undergone thermal breakdown into polar degradation products: free fatty acids, mono- and diglycerides, polymeric triglycerides, and volatile aldehydes.

cookingMethods.name: Raw Finishing / Salad Dressings
cookingMethods.description: Cold unheated usage. Zero thermal stress, preserving 100% of native heat-sensitive polyphenols, omega-3s, and aroma volatiles.

cookingMethods.name: Low-Heat Sauté / Sweating Vegetables
cookingMethods.description: Gentle skillet cooking for aromatics (onions, garlic) and delicate pan reductions. Minimal risk of triglyceride cracking.

cookingMethods.name: Medium Pan-Frying / Sautéing
cookingMethods.description: Standard stovetop skillet cooking for vegetables, eggs, chicken breasts, and tofu. Moderate heat requiring oxidative resilience.

cookingMethods.name: Deep-Frying (Continuous Submersion)
cookingMethods.description: Submerged continuous cooking (potatoes, tempura, chicken). Prolonged contact with air at high heat dramatically accelerates lipid breakdown.

cookingMethods.name: High-Heat Stir-Frying / Wok Cooking
cookingMethods.description: Fast, high-temperature cooking in a wok or cast-iron skillet. Demands high smoke point and low PUFA content to prevent acrolein plume release.

cookingMethods.name: Extreme Searing / Oven Broiling
cookingMethods.description: Ultra-high heat steak searing, cast iron blackening, and commercial broiler baking. Exceeds the smoke point of almost all unrefined cooking fats.

oils.name: Extra Virgin Olive Oil (Cold-Pressed)
oils.scientificVerdict: Exceptional oxidative stability. Modern laboratory research (De Alzaa et al., 2018) demonstrates EVOO generates significantly fewer polar compounds and toxic aldehydes during domestic cooking than high-smoke-point refined vegetable oils, because its natural polyphenols (hydroxytyrosol, oleocanthal) actively neutralize lipid peroxy radicals.

oils.name: Avocado Oil (Refined / High-Heat)
oils.scientificVerdict: The gold standard for high-temperature culinary searing. Possesses the highest reliable smoke point of any culinary vegetable oil (520°F / 271°C) combined with a monounsaturated-dominant oleic acid profile that inherently resists free radical peroxidative cascade.

oils.name: Avocado Oil (Extra Virgin / Cold-Pressed)
oils.scientificVerdict: Rich in chlorophyll, carotenoids, and lutein. Excellent antioxidant barrier against oxidation, but unrefined fruit solids lower its smoke point to around 385°F. Best for dressing and medium cooking.

oils.name: Traditional Ghee (Clarified Butter)
primaryAldehydes: Trace aldehydes only; potential cholesterol oxides if severely overheated
oils.scientificVerdict: Removing the milk solids (casein, whey, and lactose) from butter elevates the smoke point from 350°F to 485°F. Because 65% of its fatty acids are saturated and only 5% are polyunsaturated, ghee exhibits outstanding structural resilience against carcinogenic aldehyde formation under intense pan heat.

oils.name: Grass-Fed Beef Tallow
oils.scientificVerdict: A historically proven traditional frying fat with extraordinary oxidative resistance. Contains almost no vulnerable polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA 5%), preventing the formation of toxic alkenals during continuous deep-frying cycles.

oils.name: Coconut Oil (Virgin / Unrefined)
oils.scientificVerdict: Possesses over 90% saturated medium-chain fatty acids (lauric, myristic), making it chemically immune to lipid peroxidation. However, unrefined particulates smoke at 350°F, creating acrolein and particulate smoke if overheated.

oils.name: Coconut Oil (Refined / Deodorized)
oils.scientificVerdict: Refining removes free fatty acids and scent, pushing thermal tolerance up to 425°F. Generates zero measurable 4-HNE or MDA due to virtually non-existent PUFA content (2%).

oils.name: Butter (Whole / Unsalted)
oils.scientificVerdict: Contains approximately 16% water and 2% milk solids (casein and lactose). When heated above 300°F, the proteins and sugars caramelize rapidly and begin to scorch, releasing acrolein and toxic advanced lipoxidation products (ALEs). Must be clarified into ghee for high-heat cooking.

oils.name: Pure / Light Refined Olive Oil
oils.scientificVerdict: Has an elevated smoke point due to chemical refining, though at the expense of native phenolic antioxidants. Still benefits from a resilient oleic acid monounsaturated foundation, making it far superior to corn or soybean oil.

oils.name: High-Oleic Sunflower Oil
oils.scientificVerdict: Bred from specialized non-GMO sunflower cultivars to replace unstable linoleic acid with 82% oleic acid. Unlike traditional high-PUFA sunflower oil, high-oleic variants resist rancidity and produce over 75% fewer toxic aldehydes.

oils.name: Peanut Oil (Refined)
primaryAldehydes: Moderate 4-HNE and MDA on prolonged heating
oils.scientificVerdict: A classic commercial frying medium with balanced monounsaturated and polyunsaturated content. While mechanically resilient at 375°F for short durations, its 33% PUFA content will generate toxic aldehydes if reused multiple times.

oils.name: Rice Bran Oil
oils.scientificVerdict: Popular across Japanese and Asian wok cooking for its crisp finish and high smoke point. Contains gamma-oryzanol, a unique phytosterol antioxidant that delays thermal breakdown, but its 36% PUFA level warrants careful heat monitoring.

oils.name: Sesame Oil (Refined / White)
primaryAldehydes: Moderate 4-HNE and acrolein upon prolonged frying
oils.scientificVerdict: Refining neutralizes seed solids while preserving moderate levels of sesamol and sesamolin antioxidants. However, 44% polyunsaturates mean heating beyond 400°F sparks steady aldehyde cleavage.

oils.name: Toasted Sesame Oil (Finishing Oil)
oils.scientificVerdict: An aromatic finishing seasoning, NEVER a cooking medium. Microscopic toasted seed particles burn instantly in a hot wok, filling the kitchen with acrolein and scorched bitter compounds that ruin dish flavor and create toxic fumes.

oils.name: Canola / Rapeseed Oil (Refined)
oils.scientificVerdict: Contains ~10% alpha-linolenic acid (ALA, omega-3). While omega-3s are beneficial when consumed raw, their multiple double bonds are chemically hyper-fragile under thermal stress, decomposing into cytotoxic 4-HHE and acrolein fumes when heated over 375°F for extended intervals.

oils.name: Corn Oil (Refined)
oils.scientificVerdict: A textbook example of why high smoke point does NOT equate to culinary safety. With 59% linoleic acid (omega-6), heating corn oil causes rapid lipid peroxidation, producing some of the highest concentrations of toxic 4-HNE and volatile aldehydes among all common cooking fats (Prof. Martin Grootveld, DMU research).

oils.name: Soybean Oil ('Vegetable Oil' Blend)
oils.scientificVerdict: Represents the vast majority of commercial fryer and generic 'vegetable oil' bottles. Contains 61% polyunsaturated fat (54% linoleic, 7% linolenic). Repeated heating in restaurants or domestic kitchens converts this oil into a potent factory of genotoxic aldehydes and total polar polymers.

oils.name: Standard Sunflower Oil (High-Linoleic)
oils.scientificVerdict: Contains almost 70% polyunsaturated linoleic acid. Clinical lipid studies consistently rank high-linoleic sunflower oil as the worst offender for cytotoxic aldehyde generation during standard frying experiments, surpassing even lard and corn oil in total toxic volatile output.

oils.name: Grapeseed Oil
oils.scientificVerdict: Widely and erroneously promoted as a clean high-heat oil. At 74% polyunsaturated omega-6 fat, grapeseed oil has one of the lowest oxidative stability indices in existence. When heated in a hot pan, its molecular structure degrades rapidly into mutagenic polar polymers and toxic aldehydes.

oils.name: Flaxseed / Walnut Oil (Cold-Pressed)
recommendedUses: Raw Cold Finishing ONLY (Drizzling over cool porridge or salads)
oils.scientificVerdict: Contains up to 55% alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3). It is completely incapable of withstanding thermal energy. Heating flaxseed oil to even boiling water temperatures triggers immediate thermal decomposition, severe off-flavors, rancidity, trans-isomer formation, and heavy toxic aldehyde generation. Must be stored refrigerated.

reuseMultipliers.name: Reused Once (Filtered)
reuseMultipliers.riskNote: Pre-existing hydroperoxides catalyze faster degradation upon reheating.

reuseMultipliers.name: Reused Twice (Filtered)
reuseMultipliers.riskNote: Substantial breakdown into free fatty acids and polar polymers; smoke point drops 30-40°F.

reuseMultipliers.name: Reused 3+ Times (Commercial/Home)
reuseMultipliers.riskNote: Dangerous levels of total polar materials (TPM approaching or exceeding 24% limit). Carcinogenic aldehyde emissions spike dramatically.
